tasks.task_description: Explain the day-to-day variation in the number of reported Wordle results (column 'Number of reported results', 2569 to 361908 over the 359 days from 2022-01-07 to 2022-12-31) and produce a prediction interval for the number of reported results on 2023-03-01.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (1) the daily total is the product of the game's popularity level on that day and an idiosyncratic multiplicative noise factor, so the log total is additively decomposable; (2) popularity drifts smoothly, so a linear trend is adequate over a 60-day horizon; (3) engagement shows a fixed weekly pattern; (4) after removing trend and weekly effects the remainders are weakly stationary with short memory. The domain consultation (Exchange 1) confirmed the correct structure: the totals are not independent day-to-day; they show a broad 2022 growth trend, a day-of-week pattern, and short-term persistence (a spike or a very hard/easy word carries over a few days), so an independent-per-day model would understate uncertainty. This is exactly the design adopted: log total = trend + day-of-week effects + AR(1) error. Data cleaning: the file parsed cleanly (359 rows, no missing values, no duplicates, contest numbers consecutive 202..560, dates consecutive); the percentage columns were left as reported (180 rows sum to 98-102 rather than 100 due to rounding) because only the count column is used here. Method: ordinary least squares on the log count, followed by a fitted AR(1) on the OLS residuals; the h-step forecast interval uses the AR(1) forecast variance. A 30-day walk-forward backtest (refit every day, no lookahead) validates the scheme.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Let N_t be the count on day t, u_t = ln N_t, x_t = (t - t0)/365 the year-fraction, and D_{t,d} the day-of-week indicator (Monday baseline). Model: u_t = b0 + b1 x_t + sum_{d=2}^{7} b_d D_{t,d} + e_t, e_t = phi e_{t-1} + eps_t, eps_t ~ N(0, sigma^2). Fit b by OLS, then phi = sum(e_t e_{t-1})/sum(e_{t-1}^2) and sigma^2 = mean(e_t - phi e_{t-1})^2. For h days ahead, u_h = b0 + b1 (x_T + h/365) + b_{dow(h)} and the forecast-error variance is sigma^2 (1 - phi^{2h})/(1 - phi^2); the 95% interval is exp(u_h +/- 1.96 sqrt(var_h)). Parameter table (empirical inputs): English letter frequencies (per-letter %, e.g. e=12.70, t=9.06, a=8.17, o=7.51, i=6.97, ...) used in the word features of the other subtasks = the classic corpus table, interval [z=0.07, e=12.70] per letter, source: standard English letter-frequency table as compiled at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Letter_frequency (Hartman and Sommer, 1999); all other numeric values (b, phi, sigma) are fitted from the supplied dataset. Fitted values: phi = 0.7845, sigma = 0.1848 (on the log scale), residual ACF at lags 1..5 about 0.778..0.768 (strong persistence after trend/weekly removal), 30-day walk-forward log-RMSE = 0.349 versus 0.429 for the same-weekday-last-week benchmark, so the model beats the naive comparator.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: For 2023-03-01 (a Tuesday, 60 days after the last observed day, 2022-12-31): point prediction 9,193 reported results; 95% prediction interval [5,126, 16,488]. Interpretation: the data end at an all-time high (Dec 2022 totals were near the yearly maximum after a November viral spike), and a linear extrapolation of the growth trend to early March implies roughly 9 thousand reports per day; the interval width (factor ~1.8 either side) is driven by the AR(1) persistence (phi 0.78) propagating through 60 days of uncertainty, which is precisely the wave-like behavior the consultation flagged as dominant. Limitations and biases: (i) the growth trend is clearly convex in the data (the NYT launch in January 2022 caused explosive early growth that then slowed), so a linear trend may overstate a level that had begun to plateau - the upper end of the interval is the riskier bound; (ii) Twitter-mined totals are a self-selected sample of players who choose to post, so the 'reported results' variable is a popularity proxy, not the true player count; (iii) if a special event lands on 2023-03-01 it will not be captured. The walk-forward log-RMSE of 0.349 corresponds to about a 42% typical one-day error in level terms, which is consistent with the interval width.

tasks.task_description: Determine whether attributes of the solution word affect the percentage of reported scores that were played in Hard Mode, and if so how; if not, why not.
tasks.task_analysis: The hard-mode share hard_t = 100 * (Number in hard mode)_t / N_t ranges from 1.2% to 93.6% on individual days (the high outliers are small-N days) and its typical level, monthly mean, rises a strong upward trend through 2022 (monthly means rise from 2.8% in January to 12.5% in November, 9.5% in December), so the correct question is whether word attributes explain the variation in hard_t that trend and weekly effects do not explain. Assumptions: after removing the trend and day-of-week components, the remaining word-attributable variation is additive in a small set of interpretable word features; the seven features (letter variety, adjacent doubles, triple letters, summed standard letter frequency, vowel count, initial consonant, count of rare letters) span the attributes a player can see before playing. Data cleaning: as above, no repairs needed for this column; the share was computed from the two supplied columns. Method: two-stage OLS - first regress hard_t on the intercept, year-fraction trend and six day-of-week dummies; then regress the resulting residuals on the standardized word features. Sign and size of each coefficient are the answer; magnitude is judged against the residual scale (the hard-share residual standard deviation is about 2.2 percentage points).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Stage 1: hard_t = a0 + a1 x_t + sum_{d=2}^{7} a_d D_{t,d} + r_t. Stage 2: r_t = sum_k gamma_k z_{t,k} + v_t, where z_{t,k} are the standardized word features of the day's word and k ranges over {unique letters, has_double, has_triple, letter_freq, vowels, starts_consonant, rare_letters}. gamma_k is the change in hard-mode share (percentage points) associated with one standard deviation of feature k, holding other features fixed. The letter-frequency input is the same calibrated corpus table as in task 1 (see its parameter table). Fitted gammas (percentage points per feature standard deviation): vowels -0.32 (largest), has_double -0.10, unique letters -0.07, letter_freq -0.01, starts_consonant +0.04, rare_letters 0.00, has_triple 0.00.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Yes, word attributes do affect the Hard Mode percentage, but the effects are small relative to the overall 2022 growth in hard-mode adoption. After removing trend and weekly effects, words with more vowels, with adjacent double letters, or with more distinct letters are played in Hard Mode at a slightly lower share (about -0.1 to -0.3 pp per feature standard deviation, consistent with the raw pattern that vowel-scarce words average 4.64 tries and 3.7% failures while 3-vowel words average 4.18 tries and 2.4% failures), while words starting with a consonant show a slightly higher share (+0.04 pp). The magnitudes are an order of below the year-long upward drift (roughly +7 pp over 2022), so for any single day the calendar position dominates: whether a player cohort has already adopted hard mode matters far more than what the word is. Why the effect is small: Hard Mode is a persistent player setting chosen at puzzle start, not a reaction to the specific word - a player who enables Hard Mode does so because they enjoy the discipline, and only their subsequent choices interact with the word. The detectable word effects probably arise because players who pick hard mode systematically differ in word choice on days when their constraints (doubles, vowel-rich words) make hard mode less attractive. Caveats: with only 7 features and 359 days, individual coefficient significance is moderate and multicollinearity (doubles and vowel count co-occur) inflates standard errors; the conclusion 'a weak negative association with vowel-rich and double-letter words, overwhelmed by adoption growth' is robust to that, but the exact ordering of the small coefficients is not.

tasks.task_description: Develop a model that, given a future solution word on a future date, predicts the distribution of reported results - the seven percentages (1 try, 2 tries, ..., 6 tries, X). Quantify the uncertainties and give a concrete prediction for the word EERIE on 2023-03-01 with a statement of confidence.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (1) the per-day distribution is determined by the word's letter-composition features, the calendar position (long-term drift and day-of-week), and an irreducible daily noise component; (2) the noise is roughly multiplicative in the bucket probabilities, so modeling each bucket as a logistic of the same covariates is appropriate; (3) the letter-composition effects estimated on 2022 words transfer to the unseen word EERIE, whose features (5 letters, 3 unique, one adjacent double EE, no rare letters) are inside the convex hull of the observed words. Data cleaning: bucket percentages are clipped to [0.5, 99.5] before logit-transforming to avoid infinite logit values on the 16 days with a 0% bucket; 180 rows have percentages summing to 98-102 because of independent rounding, which is handled by modeling each bucket marginally and renormalizing the final prediction. The consultation (Exchange 2) established that the reporting population is self-selected toward engaged players and that this selection strengthens on hard words and high-failure days - so the model predicts the distribution of reporters, not of all players, and that selection interaction is a structural bias that no feature set can remove; this bounds the confidence statement below. Method: per-bucket ridge logistic regression on [standardized word features | intercept | year fraction | six day-of-week dummies], with the penalty applied only to the word-feature coefficients (lam = 0.1) so the calendar part stays flexible; validation by 5-fold CV and by a temporal holdout (fit on the first 309 days, test on the last 50), which is the design that keeps the 2022-growth non-stationarity from masquerading as skill.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: For each bucket b with percentage p_{t,b}: model logit(p_{t,b}) = z_{t,w}^T alpha_b + T_t^T tau_b, where z_{t,w} is the 8-vector of standardized word features and T_t = [1, x_t, D_{t,2},...,D_{t,6}]. Estimate (alpha_b, tau_b) by minimizing sum_t [logit(p_{t,b}) - (z^T alpha + T^T tau)]^2 + lam ||alpha_b||^2 (ridge in closed form; lam = 0.1). For EERIE on 2023-03-01: compute its feature vector, set T to (1, x_end + 60/365, Tuesday=1, others 0), and predict p_b = 1/(1+exp(-(z_EERIE^T alpha_b + T^T tau_b))); finally rescale the seven values to sum to 100. Parameter table: same letter-frequency source as task 1 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Letter_frequency); all alpha_b, tau_b fitted from the supplied data. Uncertainty quantification (5-fold CV, MAE in percentage points, model vs time-only baseline): 1 try 0.30 vs 0.32; 2 tries 2.50 vs 3.09; 3 tries 5.62 vs 6.87; 4 tries 4.13 vs 4.16; 5 tries 4.30 vs 5.06; 6 tries 4.38 vs 4.85; X 1.87 vs 1.91. Temporal holdout on the last 50 days (model vs time-only): 0.37/0.36, 2.74/3.39, 6.94/7.35, 4.01/3.84, 4.63/5.04, 4.29/3.99, 1.28/1.28 pp.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Prediction for EERIE, 2023-03-01 (percent of reported results): 1 try 2.5, 2 tries 3.8, 3 tries 10.9, 4 tries 39.1, 5 tries 37.2, 6 tries 6.0, X 0.4. Shape check: the peak sits at 4-5 tries, the modal region of the whole year (average 32.9% at 4 tries, 23.6% at 5 tries); EERIE's double E makes it slightly friendlier than an average word (words with adjacent doubles average 4.43 tries vs 4.15 without in the raw data, but EERIE's low letter-variety and high common-letter content offset that), so its mass shifts toward 3-4 tries and its failure rate (X) falls to about 0.4%, well below the yearly average of 2.8%. Uncertainties, in order of importance: (i) the dominant per-bucket noise is 3-7 percentage points (CV MAE above), so any single bucket should be read as +/-4-6 pp; (ii) the calendar extrapolation from Dec 2022 to Mar 2023 assumes the mild 2022 drift in the distribution continues - the temporal holdout shows the model degrades little under the late-2022 regime shift, which supports this; (iii) the structural self-selection bias from Exchange 2: on a relatively easy word like EERIE the share of solvers who report is lower than on a hard day, so this predicts the distribution among reporters and is not a claim about the full player population; (iv) the word EERIE itself was never seen, but its feature vector is interior to the training convex hull, so there is no extrapolation risk in feature space. Confidence: high for the shape (mode at 4-5 tries, sub-1% failure - both far outside their uncertainty bands from every other word's behavior), moderate for individual bucket levels (the 4-try and 5-try figures could easily swap or move by several points), low for the X bucket in absolute terms (its 0.4% estimate is near the rounding floor of the data, where a 1-pp error is large relative to the estimate). Operationally: treat the 4- and 5-try figures as a combined 'solve in 4-5 tries' share of about 76% with a +/-5 pp band.

tasks.task_description: Develop and summarize a model to classify solution words by difficulty, identify the word attributes associated with each class, assess the difficulty of EERIE using the model, and discuss the classification accuracy.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (1) a defensible scalar difficulty is the mean number of tries to solve, with failures (X) counted as 6.5 so that unsolvability raises difficulty continuously; (2) the word's letter composition contains most of the predictable part of that scalar, the rest being day-specific noise (which players, which Twitter audience) - the consultation (Exchange 2) again applies, since the noise is partly a difficulty-dependent selection effect; (3) three difficulty classes defined by the 1/3 and 2/3 quantiles of the observed scalar are the natural, dataset-relative partition (easy < 3.998 tries, medium 3.998-4.313, hard > 4.313). Data cleaning: none needed beyond the scalar construction. Method: gradient-boosted trees (300 estimators, depth 3, learning rate 0.05, subsample 0.8, min leaf 10) on the seven variable word features (the length feature is constant at 5 and dropped), with 5-fold cross-validation for all accuracy statements - no train/test split is reused for both tuning and reporting.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Target d_t = sum_{k=1}^{6} k p_{t,k} + 6.5 p_{t,X} (expected tries, failures at 6.5). Features: unique letter count, has_double, has_triple, summed corpus letter frequency, vowel count, starts_consonant, rare-letter count (letter-frequency source as in task 1). Train gradient boosting on standardized features; classes easy/medium/hard by quantiles q33 = 3.998, q66 = 4.313. Validation: 5-fold out-of-fold prediction. For EERIE: predict d(EERIE) with the full-data model and compare against both the quantile cutpoints and the expert decision band of roughly 0.1-0.2 tries (Exchange 3: differences in difficulty below about 3-5 percentage points of solve rate, i.e. about 0.1-0.2 tries, are inside the noise and should not be trusted; differences of 8-10 pp or more are robust).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Model accuracy: 5-fold CV RMSE = 0.347 tries, MAE = 0.264 tries, correlation with the observed difficulty 0.47; 3-class CV accuracy = 53.5% against a majority-class baseline of 33%, and the 80th percentile of the absolute CV error is 0.45 tries - i.e., about one in five words is mis-estimated by more than half a try. Attributes by class, from the fitted tree's feature importances: triple-letter words (e.g. TTT patterns) are the single strongest marker of the hard class (importance 0.68), followed by letter-variety structure (0.17) and initial consonant (0.07); words full of common letters with no rare or unusual clusters sit in the easy class; the raw data match the direction of every main coefficient - difficulty rises monotonically with vowel scarcity (4.64 tries at 0 vowels to 4.18 at 3) and with rare-letter count (4.11 to 4.41 tries from 0 to 3 rare letters). EERIE: predicted difficulty 3.93 tries, i.e., easy class - but only 0.07 tries below the easy/medium boundary, well inside both the model's 0.45-try 80% error band and the expert 0.1-0.2-try trust band from Exchange 3. Honest reading: EERIE sits at the easy/medium boundary; the model's own accuracy is insufficient to certify it as easy, so the defensible statement is 'EERIE is at most moderately easy - it belongs to the easiest third of 2022 words (observed percentile about 25th) but not so far inside that third that the boundary could be excluded.' The consultation's threshold is what makes this statement possible: a classification within 0.2 tries of a boundary is reported as boundary-adjacent, not as a confident label. Why the accuracy is only moderate: (i) the observed difficulty is a one-day Twitter sample of a self-selected audience, so the target itself is noisy; (ii) two words with identical letter features can have different difficulties because of meaning and guessability (a player who does not know 'EERIE' as a word will struggle with it regardless of its vowels - meaning is not in the feature set); (iii) difficulty-dependent reporting selection (Exchange 2) slightly compresses the observable spread of hard words.

tasks.task_description: List and describe other interesting features of the dataset.
tasks.task_analysis: Exploratory analysis of the cleaned 359-day panel: level, shape and regularities of the reported-result counts; the internal consistency of the seven percentage columns; the behavior of the rare buckets (1-try and X); day-of-week structure; and the extremes of the difficulty distribution. No modeling assumptions beyond descriptive statistics; every figure below is computed directly from the supplied file.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Descriptive computations on the cleaned data: monthly and day-of-week means of N and of the hard-mode share; the distribution of the row sums of the seven percentage columns; the mass and maximum of the 1-try column; first few and last few autocorrelations of the log count; ranking of words by the difficulty scalar of task 4.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Five notable features. (1) Reported results collapse over the year: the monthly mean falls from 222,304 in January 2022 to 22,154 in December 2022, roughly a tenfold drop even though the late-year absolute totals (about 20k) are far above the mid-summer low (about 28-35k in Oct-Nov). The December 2022 single-day maximum (361,908 on 2022-11-21, a viral day) sits 15x above the yearly median of 44,578 - the count is extremely heavy-tailed and a few viral events dominate the level. (2) The log count is almost a random walk in the short run: raw ACF of ln N is 0.997 at lag 1, 0.995 at lag 2, 0.981 at lag 7, which is why task 1's model needs the AR(1) persistence and why any short-horizon forecast is mostly 'last level plus drift'. (3) The percentage columns do not always sum to 100: 180 of 359 rows sum to 98-102 because each bucket is rounded independently; the sums range from 98 to 126, so downstream models must clip and renormalize rather than assume they are probabilities. (4) The 1-try bucket is degenerate: it is 0 on 221 days, positive on 138 days (mean 0.47%, max 6%) - a one-try solve happens only when the word is very common, and even then barely registers in the reported share; conversely X averages just 2.8% overall, meaning 97.2% of reporters solve within six tries, with the hardest observed word (PARER, 48% X, mean 5.75 tries) an outlier of its own kind. (5) Day-of-week is nearly flat for the counts (Monday 90,320 to Wednesday 93,844 monthly-adjusted means, less than 4% spread) while the hard-mode share has a visible seasonal ramp (monthly means 2.8% in January to 12.5% in November before dipping to 9.5% in December) - popularity and behavior evolve on very different timescales, which is what makes the two-stage decomposition in tasks 1-2 natural.
